clue.text: First-class accommodation provided by Ludwig Bemelmans

definitions.text: First-class accommodation provided by Ludwig Bemelmans

parts.words: First-class accommodation provided by Ludwig Bemelmans
parts.note: a grand place to stay, and also the title of Ludwig Bemelmans's 1946 book of stories about working in a smart New York establishment, completed by the light at 4

explanation.surface: A luxury place to stay laid on by the writer Ludwig Bemelmans.
explanation.walkthrough: This light and 4 across together give the title of Bemelmans's book; this entry is the first word, the kind of building where guests stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bemelmans's book title names a splendid inn for travellers, so first-class lodging is exactly what the first word denotes.

clue.text: Rhyme "push" inaccurately for Welsh poet

indicators.note: written inaccurately, the letters of the two words rhyme and push come out in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone rhymes the word push badly while writing about a poet from Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Emyr Humphreys was a Welsh novelist and poet writing in English.

clue.text: "I met wid Napper —, and he took me by the hand" (The Wearin' O' The Green)

definitions.text: "I met wid Napper —, and he took me by the hand" (The Wearin' O' The Green)

parts.words: "I met wid Napper —, and he took me by the hand" (The Wearin' O' The Green)
parts.note: a line from the Irish rebel ballad, with the surname of the United Irishman James Napper left blank

explanation.surface: A line from an Irish street ballad about meeting a rebel leader.
explanation.definitionFit: James Napper, the Irish revolutionary of 1798, is the figure named in the ballad's famous line.

clue.text: Amaze a piece by Borges, say

explanation.surface: Astonish someone with a story by Borges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amaze' is read as A MAZE; Borges's best-known collection in English is Labyrinths.
explanation.definitionFit: A maze is a bewildering network of paths, and Borges wrote stories built on endless winding passages, collected as Labyrinths.

clue.text: See 1

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'See 1': second word of HOTEL SPLENDIDE, but the puzzle file records no group linking it to 1-across, so it cannot be annotated on its leader

clue.text: Playschool is an outrage

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a nursery school is shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playschool' points to Sheridan's comedy The School for ___: the play's school exists for this.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's play is The School for gossip and disgrace, and a public outrage is a disgraceful affair.

clue.text: Lady (sic) upset in sad work by Milton

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of lady and sic are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman is upset by a sorrowful poem by Milton.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's pastoral elegy of 1637 mourns his drowned Cambridge friend Edward King.

clue.text: Conventional interior of casino Mickey Spillane depicted

indicators.note: the inside of the phrase casino Mickey holds the letters, spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A conventional casino scene of the kind the thriller writer Mickey Spillane depicted.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomic is a rare word meaning customary or conventional, used of ordinary spelling as opposed to phonetic.

clue.text: What Stevie Smith became to see the person from Porlock

definitions.text: What Stevie Smith became to see the person from Porlock

parts.words: What Stevie Smith became to see the person from Porlock
parts.note: her poem Thoughts about the Person from Porlock says she longs for the visitor who interrupted Coleridge to come and interrupt her

explanation.surface: A question about how the poet Stevie Smith felt about Coleridge's famous interrupter.
explanation.definitionFit: Smith writes that she is hungry to be interrupted, eager and restless for the visitor's arrival.

clue.text: Sign of the beast in Handel and Bach

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the words Handel and, across the gap

explanation.surface: A musical motif for the animal appears in Handel and in Bach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign of the' is surface; the beast is an African antelope.
explanation.definitionFit: The eland is the largest African antelope, a big wild animal.

clue.text: Peak of Shelley's achievement

explanation.surface: The finest thing Shelley ever accomplished.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest summit in the Alps is a peak, and Shelley wrote a celebrated 1816 poem with that mountain's name as its title.

clue.text: A cuckoo to Pamela's nightingale, according to Sir Philip Sidney

definitions.text: A cuckoo to Pamela's nightingale, according to Sir Philip Sidney

parts.words: A cuckoo to Pamela's nightingale, according to Sir Philip Sidney
parts.note: in Sidney's Arcadia the lovely princess Pamela is set beside a coarse, foolish young woman of the shepherd's family, compared as a harsh bird against a sweet singer

explanation.surface: A literary comparison of two birds, credited to the Elizabethan poet Sidney.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Arcadia the shepherd Dametas's ugly daughter is the comic foil to the princess, the cuckoo against the nightingale.

clue.text: Her material was historical, romantic. Also georgette

definitions.text: Her material was historical, romantic. Also georgette

parts.words: Her material was historical, romantic. Also georgette
parts.note: reads like a description of a fabric, georgette being a thin crêpe, but points to the English novelist Georgette whose stories were Regency romances

explanation.surface: A dressmaker describes a fabric that was both historic and romantic, and also a crêpe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' and 'georgette' suggest cloth; the clue really describes a novelist named Georgette and the historical romances that were her subject matter.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer Georgette of that surname produced Regency romances, so historical romance was her literary material.

clue.text: What many books are, without being especially wholehearted

explanation.surface: Many books are devoted to someone without their being especially devoted.
explanation.definitionFit: Books often open with a dedication to a person, and a devoted, committed worker is wholehearted.

clue.text: Sort of Footman that held Prufrock's coat

definitions.text: Sort of Footman that held Prufrock's coat

parts.words: Sort of Footman that held Prufrock's coat
parts.note: in Eliot's Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock the speaker has seen death, personified as a servant lasting for ever, hold his coat and snicker

explanation.surface: A question about which servant helped Eliot's Prufrock with his coat.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's line describes an everlasting servant, a figure of death, so the adjective means lasting for all time.

clue.text: Suite provided by Cameron Hawley

parts.note: Cameron Hawley's 1952 business novel, filmed in 1954, is titled after the boardroom offices of a company's top management

explanation.surface: A set of rooms supplied by the writer Cameron Hawley.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawley's novel title pairs the word for senior management with suite, the offices of company directors.

clue.text: Foster mother to speedy Arcadian heroine

definitions.text: Foster mother to speedy Arcadian heroine

parts.words: Foster mother to speedy Arcadian heroine
parts.note: Atalanta, the swift-footed huntress of Arcadia, was left on a mountainside as a baby and suckled by a female wild animal

explanation.surface: Who raised the fleet-footed girl from Arcadia in the old myth?
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the abandoned Atalanta was nursed by a female bear sent by Artemis, which became her foster parent.

clue.text: Byzantine governorships possibly cheer Axis

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of cheer and Axis may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Byzantine provinces might be cheered by the wartime Axis powers.
explanation.definitionFit: An exarch governed a distant province of the Byzantine empire, such as Ravenna or Carthage, and his domain took the related name.

clue.text: His poems came from an exclusive quarter of New York

definitions.text: His poems came from an exclusive quarter of New York

parts.words: His poems came from an exclusive quarter of New York
parts.note: Morris, the Yiddish sweatshop poet, wrote from the crowded Jewish immigrant Lower East Side, exclusive in an ironic sense

explanation.surface: A poet whose verse came out of a smart, select district of Manhattan.
explanation.definitionFit: Morris Rosenfeld's Yiddish poems of sweatshop life came from the immigrant ghetto of the Lower East Side.

clue.text: Thackeray's son-in-law, fathered Woolf

parts.note: Sir Leslie, editor and critic, married Thackeray's daughter Minny and later fathered Virginia Woolf by his second wife

explanation.surface: A Victorian man of letters who married into Thackeray's family and was Virginia Woolf's father.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Leslie, first editor of the Dictionary of National Biography, carried this surname, which Virginia bore before marriage.

clue.text: … from the snare of the hunter: and from the pestilence" (Prayer Book)

definitions.text: … from the snare of the hunter: and from the pestilence" (Prayer Book)

parts.words: … from the snare of the hunter: and from the pestilence" (Prayer Book)
parts.note: Psalm 91 in the Book of Common Prayer, with the adjective describing the deadly plague left blank

explanation.surface: A quotation from the psalms about rescue from traps and disease.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prayer Book psalm calls the plague harmful and foul, the sense of this old adjective.

clue.text: Comic writer who found his plots in the attic

definitions.text: Comic writer who found his plots in the attic

parts.words: Comic writer who found his plots in the attic
parts.note: the Roman comedian adapted Greek New Comedy from Athens, so his plots came from Attic, Athenian, originals, not a loft

explanation.surface: A funny author rummaging upstairs in the loft for story ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attic' is not a loft but the adjective for Athens: the Roman playwright reworked Greek comedies by Menander and others.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman playwright behind Pseudolus and Miles Gloriosus wrote comedies adapted from Athenian originals.

clue.text: Cornish squire heard to have canvassed ship

indicators.note: heard means the clue words are spoken and the sound gives the entry

parts.note: canvassed means polled, as voters are, and a ship can be an ark

explanation.surface: A Cornish landowner is said to have sought votes from a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Ross Poldark is the hero of Winston Graham's novels set in 18th-century Cornwall, later a TV series.
explanation.definitionFit: Winston Graham's hero Ross is a Cornish gentleman landowner and mine owner.

clue.text: War correspondent turned historian (with other talents in reserve)

definitions.text: War correspondent turned historian (with other talents in reserve)

parts.words: War correspondent turned historian (with other talents in reserve)
parts.note: Winston reported the Boer War for the Morning Post, later wrote histories, and was also painter, bricklayer and prime minister

explanation.surface: A journalist from the front who became a historian, keeping other skills up his sleeve.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis hints at the statesman's painting, Nobel prize and premiership behind the journalist and historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Winston reported the Boer War as a journalist and later wrote multi-volume histories, among many other talents.

clue.text: Succession, say, for Demeter

indicators.note: say means the word is spoken, so its sound gives the entry

parts.note: a succession of things is a series

explanation.surface: A line of events, perhaps, for the Greek goddess of the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman goddess is the counterpart of the Greek Demeter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman corn goddess is identified with Demeter, her Greek equivalent.

clue.text: Governor of Tarsus discovers the French in swindle

indicators.note: in places the French article inside the word for swindle

parts.note: a con is a swindle
le is the French masculine definite article

explanation.surface: A provincial governor discovers French people involved in a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Pericles, Cleon rules Tarsus and later plots against Marina.

clue.text: Falstaff said to have sold his soul for its leg and some Madeira

definitions.text: Falstaff said to have sold his soul for its leg and some Madeira

parts.words: Falstaff said to have sold his soul for its leg and some Madeira
parts.note: in Henry IV Part 1 Poins says Falstaff sold his soul to the devil for a cup of Madeira and a cold leg of a fattened bird

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's fat knight is accused of trading his soul for a joint of meat and a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Poins's jibe names a castrated cockerel fattened for the table, whose cold leg Falstaff supposedly bargained for.

clue.text: Animosity encountered in Mrs Battle's favourite card game for two

indicators.note: the feeling is met inside the name of the card game, which loses its final letter

parts.words: Mrs Battle's favourite card game for two
parts.note: Mrs Battle in Charles Lamb's essay loves whist, but piquet is the two-handed game she also favours

explanation.surface: Bad feeling arises during the card game an old lady in Lamb loved best.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist is an essay by Charles Lamb; the game's name, minus its last letter T, gives the resentment.
explanation.definitionFit: Pique is resentment from wounded pride, a form of hostility.

clue.text: "— High The Roof Beam, Carpenters"

parts.note: the title of J. D. Salinger's novella about the Glass family, with its opening verb left blank

explanation.surface: A call to builders to lift a roof timber, the title of a Salinger book.
explanation.definitionFit: Salinger's title, borrowed from Sappho, begins with the verb meaning to lift up.

clue.text: Carelessly lose a quid naming inhabitant of seraglio

indicators.note: doing something carelessly leaves it in a muddle, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone carelessly loses a pound while naming a harem dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: A female slave or concubine in an Ottoman harem; the seraglio is the harem quarters.

clue.text: Measure of German lager by the stream for novelist

parts.note: a stein is a large German beer mug, so a measure of lager
beck is a northern English word for a stream or brook

explanation.surface: A mug of German beer drunk beside the brook, recommended for a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: BECK is a dialect word from northern England for a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: John Steinbeck was the American author of The Grapes of Wrath and Of Mice and Men.

clue.text: New Zealand critic gets dates mixed

indicators.note: mixed up means the letters of the word dates are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A critic from New Zealand gets his diary dates muddled.
explanation.definitionFit: C. K. Stead is a leading New Zealand poet, novelist and literary critic.
